cultivar: Ukrainian subpopulation of Georgian Camellia sinensis
processing: The small modern batches are made as a strongly oxidised oolong by the enthusiast tending the plot; green or black tea would be possible from the same leaf.
harvest_season: Twice a year, in early May and late June. Yield is tiny and depends on drought and heat.
appearance_dry: As with other strongly oxidised oolongs, dark twisted leaf, though little is published on the appearance of this batch.
appearance_liquor: Likely amber, as is typical of strongly oxidised oolong; few people have seen it.
appearance_wet: Not documented; the bushes are genetically varied, so leaves vary in density and length.
taste_profile: Described in general terms as a broad aroma with many floral notes, changing from year to year with the leaf.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a strongly oxidised oolong. No specific brewing advice exists for this tea, which very few people will ever brew.

vintage_note: Not on sale: the keeper of the plot says the project is non-commercial, and each year's batch, about 200 g in a recent year, goes to a tasting for professionals in Kyiv. Each year differs with the weather. Anything sold as Mukachevo tea deserves suspicion, and a small farm remains only a proposal.
description:
Mukachevo tea comes from a tiny surviving patch of tea bushes in a beech forest beside Red Mountain, near Mukachevo in far western Ukraine. It was long called the northernmost tea plantation in Europe, a claim worth taking loosely. It exists mainly as a curiosity and a rescue project.

The bushes descend from Georgian plants. Decades of neglect left them overgrown. About 350 are now tended, with winter covers and added humus, and their genetic mix is thought to help them survive. The enthusiast Maksym Malyhin makes the leaf into an oolong named Red Shar'kan, after the mountain.

The taste is reported only in broad terms: wide aromas with floral notes, and clear differences between years. A Kyiv tasting panel rated the 2024 batch highly.

You cannot really buy it. The harvest reached up to 4 kg of fresh leaf in 2025 and has fallen to a few hundred grams in bad years. You can visit, though: a marked trail leads to the site, and the bushes should be left alone, since visitors have stripped leaves and dug up plants that almost never survive being moved.
history:
Tea growing here was a Soviet experiment after the Second World War, which followed botanical work on acclimatising tea under Professor Viktor Sochava. Accounts of the date conflict: one local account gives spring 1949 for the planting, another 1945, and collective farms are recorded laying out about 50 hectares in 1951 and 1952 and 75 hectares by 1954. The bushes grew and gave usable leaf, but the work was dropped after Stalin's death in 1953. Only a small plot in the forest survived.

Maksym Malyhin began caring for the neglected patch about a decade ago. In 2019 volunteers cleared brambles and saplings from part of it, and small batches of oolong are made there now.
